---
title: "3. Pricing by Euler equation"
---

Part I ended with a diagnosis. A discounted-cash-flow valuation has two
free numbers — a growth rate and a discount rate — and nothing inside
the method disciplines either one ([Chapter 1](01-two-free-numbers.qmd)).
And the data contain a spread the standard repair does not price: value
portfolios have out-earned growth portfolios by about six points a year
while their market betas point the wrong way
([Chapter 2](02-value-premium-in-the-data.qmd)). This chapter begins the
rebuild. It replaces the two free numbers with one equation and one
economic object.

The equation says that an investor who can buy a little more or a
little less of any asset must, at her chosen consumption plan, be
indifferent to doing so. That indifference condition prices the asset.
No forecasting skill enters, no exogenous discount rate is assumed;
the price falls out of the investor's willingness to trade consumption
today for consumption in each possible state tomorrow.

The generality is the point, and it is why this course is called
*valuing asset claims* rather than valuing stocks. The same condition,
with the same economic object inside it, prices a broad stock
portfolio, a Treasury bill, a value portfolio, and the dividend stream
of a private firm that has never traded. The machine does not care
what the claim is called. It cares only about what the claim's payoffs
covary with.

The chapter then puts the simplest version of that object — the
power-utility kernel that most of macroeconomics runs on — in front of
74 years of data and watches it fail three times. Those three failures
are the reason [Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) changes the
preferences and [Chapter 5](05-long-run-risks.qmd) changes the
endowment.

## One equation, every claim

For any traded claim $i$ with gross return $R_{i,t+1}$, the first-order
condition of an investor's consumption–portfolio problem is

$$
E_t\!\left[M_{t+1}\, R_{i,t+1}\right] = 1 .
$$ {#eq-euler}

$M_{t+1}$ is the **pricing kernel** (also called the stochastic
discount factor, or the intertemporal marginal rate of substitution):
the rate at which the investor is willing to exchange consumption at
$t$ for consumption in each state at $t+1$. It is high in states where
the investor is desperate — where marginal utility is high — and low in
states where she is flush. Equation @eq-euler says that once payoffs
are weighted by that state-by-state exchange rate, every asset earns
exactly its price: no claim is a free lunch relative to the investor's
own marginal utility.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Derivation: the Euler equation from a consumption choice"}
Let the investor maximize $E_t \sum_j \delta^j u(C_{t+j})$ and consider
a perturbation: reduce consumption at $t$ by a small amount $\xi$, buy
$\xi/P_t$ units of an asset with price $P_t$ and payoff $X_{t+1}$, and
consume the proceeds. At an optimum the perturbation cannot improve
welfare in either direction, so the marginal cost equals the marginal
benefit: $u'(C_t)\,P_t = E_t[\delta\, u'(C_{t+1})\, X_{t+1}]$. Divide
by $u'(C_t)$ and by $P_t$, and define
$M_{t+1} = \delta\, u'(C_{t+1})/u'(C_t)$ and
$R_{i,t+1} = X_{t+1}/P_t$; the result is @eq-euler. Nothing in the
argument used what the asset *is* — only that the investor could hold a
little more or less of it. The same $M$ therefore prices every claim
she can trade, and prices a non-traded dividend stream by the value at
which she would be indifferent to holding it.
:::

Written in price form, $P_t = E_t[M_{t+1} X_{t+1}]$: today's price is
the payoff in each state, weighted by probability *and* by how much a
unit of payoff is worth in that state. A DCF collapses that weighted
sum into a single discount rate. The Euler equation keeps the states
separate, which is exactly where the risk adjustment lives.

Two immediate consequences organize everything that follows. Applied to
a riskless claim, whose return is known at $t$, @eq-euler gives

$$
R_{f,t} = \frac{1}{E_t[M_{t+1}]} ,
$$ {#eq-rf}

so the level of the kernel pins the risk-free rate. And subtracting the
riskless version from the risky one turns @eq-euler into a statement
about premia:

$$
E_t[R_{i,t+1}] - R_{f,t} = -R_{f,t}\,\mathrm{Cov}_t\!\left(M_{t+1},\, R_{i,t+1}\right) .
$$ {#eq-premium}

Every risk premium is a covariance with the kernel. A claim commands a
high expected return if and only if it pays badly in the states where
$M$ is high — when the investor is already hurting. A claim that pays
well in those states is insurance, and its premium is negative,
whatever its volatility. Volatility per se earns nothing; only the
covariance is priced. This one line is what the CAPM approximates (with
the market return standing in for $-M$) and what the rest of this
course computes exactly.

## The simplest kernel

To use @eq-premium quantitatively we need a concrete $M$. The workhorse
is time-separable power utility, $u(C) = C^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)$, for
which

$$
M_{t+1} = \delta \left(\frac{C_{t+1}}{C_t}\right)^{-\gamma} .
$$ {#eq-crra}

Marginal utility is high when consumption growth is low, so @eq-crra
says: an asset is risky exactly insofar as it pays badly in
consumption recessions. With jointly lognormal consumption growth and
returns, @eq-premium becomes (in logs, up to a Jensen term) the
back-of-envelope

$$
E[r_i] - r_f \approx \gamma\, \mathrm{Cov}(\Delta c,\, r_i),
$$ {#eq-boe}

and the volatility of the kernel bounds every attainable Sharpe ratio —
Hansen and Jagannathan (1991):
$\left|E[R_i] - R_f\right| / \sigma(R_i) \le \sigma(M)/E[M] \approx \gamma\,\sigma(\Delta c)$.
Aggregate consumption growth is smooth, so unless $\gamma$ is large the
kernel barely moves, and a kernel that barely moves cannot generate
large premia. That arithmetic is the equity premium puzzle of Mehra and
Prescott (1985). The next section runs it on this course's own sample.

## Hands-on: the kernel meets 74 years of data

The cells below use the three annual series built in Part I:
real consumption growth, the real T-bill, and returns on the growth,
value, and market claims.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
# Data bootstrap: use the repo's committed CSVs, or fetch them when this
# notebook runs outside the repository.
from pathlib import Path
import urllib.request

DATA = Path("../../data")
if not DATA.exists():
    DATA = Path("data")
    DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    base = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tlorans/"
            "kiku-value-premium-replication/main/data/")
    for f in ("consumption_annual.csv", "rf_annual.csv", "annual_panel.csv"):
        if not (DATA / f).exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + f, DATA / f)
```

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

cons = pd.read_csv(DATA / "consumption_annual.csv")
rf = pd.read_csv(DATA / "rf_annual.csv")
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA / "annual_panel.csv")

rets = panel.pivot(index="year", columns="claim", values="ret")
df = rets.join(rf.set_index("year")).join(cons.set_index("year"))
print(f"{len(df)} annual observations, {df.index.min()}-{df.index.max()}")
print(f"consumption growth: mean {df.dc.mean():.2%}, sd {df.dc.std():.2%}")
print(f"real T-bill:        mean {df.rf.mean():.2%}")
```

The endowment is smooth — consumption growth moves about two points a
year — and the real bill earns roughly nothing. Now the premia the
kernel has to explain:

```{python}
for name in ("Growth", "Value", "Market"):
    ex = df[name] - df.rf
    print(f"{name:8s} mean excess {ex.mean():6.2%}   "
          f"sd {ex.std():6.2%}   Sharpe {ex.mean() / ex.std():.2f}")
```

Feed these into @eq-boe with a conventional risk aversion of
$\gamma = 10$:

```{python}
gamma = 10.0
for name in ("Growth", "Value", "Market"):
    ex = df[name] - df.rf
    cov = np.cov(ex, df.dc, ddof=1)[0, 1]
    print(f"{name:8s} actual {ex.mean():6.2%}   "
          f"power utility, gamma=10: {gamma * cov:6.2%}")

ex_m = df["Market"] - df.rf
cov_m = np.cov(ex_m, df.dc, ddof=1)[0, 1]
print(f"\ngamma needed to match the market premium: "
      f"{ex_m.mean() / cov_m:.0f}")
```

Three failures, in order of severity.

**The equity premium puzzle.** The market earned 8.45 percent over
bills; the power-utility kernel with $\gamma = 10$ delivers 0.54
percent. Closing the gap by brute force takes $\gamma \approx 155$ —
an investor who would decline gambles no one declines. This is Mehra
and Prescott (1985) on this sample.

**The risk-free rate puzzle.** Even the *least* demanding fix fails.
The Hansen–Jagannathan bound only asks the kernel to be volatile enough
to support the market's Sharpe ratio, and then @eq-rf reports what that
volatility does to the interest rate:

```{python}
sr = ex_m.mean() / ex_m.std()
gamma_hj = sr / df.dc.std()
delta_annual = 0.999 ** 12
rf_implied = (-np.log(delta_annual) + gamma_hj * df.dc.mean()
              - gamma_hj**2 * df.dc.std()**2 / 2)
print(f"market Sharpe ratio {sr:.2f}  =>  "
      f"gamma >= {sr:.2f}/{df.dc.std():.4f} = {gamma_hj:.0f}")
print(f"risk-free rate implied by gamma = {gamma_hj:.0f}: "
      f"{rf_implied:.1%}   (data: {df.rf.mean():.2%})")
```

A $\gamma$ of 18 rescues the Sharpe ratio but predicts a 23 percent
risk-free rate against 0.07 percent in the data: an investor that
averse to risk, forced by power utility to be equally averse to
consumption *growth*, demands an enormous reward to lend into a growing
economy.

**The value premium.** The deepest failure is not about levels but
about the cross section, and no choice of $\gamma$ touches it. Look at
the $\gamma = 10$ column again: growth is assigned 0.43 percent, value
$-0.02$ percent. Value's excess return covaries with contemporaneous
consumption growth essentially not at all — the point estimate is
negative — so @eq-boe assigns the highest-earning claim in the sample a
premium of *zero at any risk aversion*. Scaling $\gamma$ up scales all
three predictions together and can never produce the six-point spread.
The one-period consumption covariance is measuring the wrong risk.

That last sentence is the agenda for the rest of Part II. The premium
must still be a covariance with the kernel — @eq-premium is not
negotiable — so the kernel must respond to something other than this
year's consumption. [Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) builds
preferences under which news about *future* consumption enters marginal
utility today, and [Chapter 5](05-long-run-risks.qmd) builds an
endowment in which there is persistent news to be had.

## Takeaways

- One condition prices every claim: $E_t[M_{t+1}R_{i,t+1}] = 1$. The
  same kernel values a stock index, a bill, and a private dividend
  stream — the machine is general, only the cash flows change.
- Premia are covariances (@eq-premium): a claim is risky if it pays
  badly when marginal utility is high. Volatility alone earns nothing.
- The power-utility kernel fails three ways on 74 years of data: the
  market premium needs $\gamma \approx 155$; a $\gamma$ large enough
  for the Sharpe ratio implies a 23 percent risk-free rate; and value's
  consumption covariance is zero, so no $\gamma$ prices the value
  premium.
- The fix cannot be a bigger $\gamma$. The kernel must price a
  different risk.

## Exercises

1. Compute the value-minus-growth spread's mean, volatility, and Sharpe
   ratio from `annual_panel.csv`. What kernel volatility
   $\sigma(M)/E[M]$ does the Hansen–Jagannathan bound demand for that
   claim alone, and what $\gamma$ does that imply?
2. Rerun the $\gamma = 10$ cell with $\gamma = 50$ and $\gamma = 155$.
   Verify that the *ratio* of the predicted value premium to the
   predicted growth premium never moves. Why not?
3. Using @eq-rf under lognormality,
   $r_f = -\log\delta + \gamma E[\Delta c] - \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma^2\sigma^2(\Delta c)$,
   solve for the $\delta$ that reconciles $\gamma = 155$ with the
   observed 0.07 percent real rate. Is it a discount factor a patient
   investor could have?
